rv.q: King of the Yees is one of the most big-hearted plays I've seen in a while...
It is remarkable how the playwright is able to pack so many aspects of her cultural heritage so easily within a surprisingly traditional father-and-daughter story.
And yes, King of the Yees does dip toward the sentimental at the end. But it's so clever, so metatheatrical, and so affectionate throughout that I hardly minded.
King of the Yees is less of a traditional family play and more of a formal experiment, one that's at times confounding but never boring, and sure to leave you with more questions than answers.

The rehearsal never seems to get back on track. There are a subsequent series of scenes between the two “actors” (Shih and Sebastian) that are not quite comic routines, but close to it; at one point, she admits she is actually Korean, and so he teaches her to say “Chinese” like a Chinese person would.
Act 2 moves like a freight train, but director Joshua Kahan Brody doesn't let things get out of control.
There are also a good many lulls between the jokes, and sequences that seem more clever in conception than execution.

cn.t: Critics praise Yee's meta-theatrical comedy as feisty and inventive, with its playful exploration of Chinese American identity earning mostly positive reviews. Some find the hazy, carnival-like structure confusing, but most appreciate its bold theatrical approach.
